echoes.note: Becoming 'partakers of the divine nature' having escaped corruption draws on the creation of humanity in God's image and likeness — the restoration of the image is the goal of the divine promises.
'I said, you are gods, sons of the Most High' is the scriptural datum behind the deifying participation language of v.4.

Wisdom's sorites, ascending from desire of instruction to love and incorruption that 'brings one near to God,' is the closest Second-Temple model for Peter's chain of virtues beginning here and listed in vv.5-7.

The graded virtue-chain ('in faith supply moral excellence; and in moral excellence, knowledge…') follows the sapiential sorites-form most fully developed in Wisdom 6, where one virtue leads to the next and finally to nearness to God.
The contrast of being 'not idle nor unfruitful' versus barrenness recalls the prophetic vineyard expected to bear fruit; a faint coherence with the fruitfulness theme.
'Make your calling and election sure' presupposes Israel's election as a chosen people, the covenant language Peter applies to the church's assurance.
'As long as I am in this tent… the putting off of my tent comes swiftly' uses the body-as-tent figure of Hezekiah's lament, 'my dwelling is plucked up and removed from me like a shepherd's tent.'
'The perishable body weighs down the soul, and this earthy tent burdens the mind' is the Hellenistic-Jewish source of the tent-of-the-body image Peter uses for his approaching death.
The Transfiguration voice 'This is my beloved Son' fuses the royal-enthronement decree 'You are my Son' with the beloved-son language; Peter cites it as eyewitness confirmation of Christ's majesty.
'In whom I am well pleased' reflects the Servant call, 'my chosen, in whom my soul delights,' the second strand woven into the heavenly voice.
'Your son, your only son… whom you love' supplies the 'beloved Son' resonance, with the Aqedah lurking behind the Father's word over Jesus.
'The holy mountain' and the voice from 'the Majestic Glory' recall Sinai, where the glory of the LORD settled on the mountain and God spoke from the cloud.
'A lamp shining in a dark place' applies the psalm's 'your word is a lamp to my feet' to the prophetic word the readers do well to heed until the day dawns.
'The morning star arises in your hearts' draws on Balaam's oracle, 'a star shall come out of Jacob,' the messianic star of dawn (cf. Malachi 4:2, the sun of righteousness).

'No prophecy ever came by the will of man, but holy men spoke being moved by the Holy Spirit' rests on David's claim, 'The Spirit of the LORD speaks by me; his word is on my tongue' — the model of Spirit-carried prophecy.
Balaam, on whom 'the Spirit of God came,' uttering the oracle of 'one who hears the words of God,' is a further instance of prophecy that comes not by human will but by the Spirit.
